description: Somos un equipo multidisciplinario apasionado por la tecnología, la Inteligencia Artificial, la Ciencia de Datos y la exploración espacial. Nos interesa convertir datos y problemas reales en soluciones innovadoras utilizando programación, IA, análisis de datos y visualización.
summary:
Before astronauts build a base at the lunar south pole or drill for ice on Mars, they practice in places on Earth that behave like those worlds. But these analog sites are rarely compared with their destination using numbers, and few teams look for new ones.

Earth Analogs compares the Moon, Mars and 45 places on Earth using the same 15 characteristics, all measured with open data: 25 years of NASA POWER climate, relief from LRO LOLA, MGS MOLA and Copernicus, ice from LRO Diviner and Mars Odyssey, ground temperature and vegetation from MODIS, JAXA ALOS PALSAR radar, ESA WorldCover and Macrostrat geologic maps.

In a guided 3D journey, you choose a base site and a mission, fly back to Earth and land on its best twin. The verdict explains why that place matches and what it cannot simulate. The app also shows where NASA already trains and how those sites rank, finds places nobody uses yet, combines 3 sites that together cover up to 96% of a destination, maps the whole planet by similarity, and measures any point on Earth live.

Choosing the right place to practice saves time, money and risk before a crew leaves Earth.
details:
What it does

Earth Analogs answers one question for mission planners, scientists and students: which place on Earth is the best rehearsal for this Moon or Mars base, for this mission, and what can it not rehearse? You register as a crew member (commander, geologist or engineer), choose a base site (3 on the Moon, 6 on Mars) and a mission (ISRU, caves, habitat, mobility, astrobiology, polar power or general), and fly back to Earth while mission control runs the analysis. The ship lands on the best twin and the verdict panel explains the result. A guided tour, a final quiz and a mission certificate help first-time users learn as they go.

How it works

1. Earth's climate. NASA POWER climatology gives six characteristics: aridity (PRECTOTCORR and RH2M), cold (T2M), daily temperature swing (T2M_RANGE), thin air (PS corrected to the real elevation), sun and UV exposure (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN and UV index) and seasonal light (darkest vs brightest month). Relief comes from the Copernicus GLO-90 elevation model.

2. The Moon and Mars, measured. We process raw NASA PDS data. Relief uses the same metric on all three worlds: LRO LOLA on the Moon and MGS MOLA on Mars. Lunar ice and cold come from the LRO Diviner Polar Resource Product: at Shackleton, ice is stable within 1 m of the surface in 35% of the area, at 120 K. Martian ice comes from the Mars Odyssey neutron map and SHARAD radar results. Seasonal light comes from an orbital model that uses the same formula on Earth. Where the Moon or Mars go beyond anything on Earth (vacuum, extreme cold, radiation), we use rover and orbiter measurements (REMS, MEDA, RAD, LADEE, CRaTER) and cap the value at Earth's most extreme place.

3. Every number shows its source. The Evidence tab labels each value as measured, geologic map, mission data or literature.

4. Similarity score. 100 × (1 − weighted distance) across the 15 characteristics. Each mission gives more weight to what it needs.

5. Untapped analogs. A second ranking rewards good matches that almost nobody uses yet.

6. Campaign builder. A coverage algorithm picks 3 sites that complement each other. What remains uncovered is what Earth cannot reproduce.

7. Live scan. Tap any point on the globe, choose a site from a list or type coordinates. The browser queries NASA POWER, the elevation model, MODIS (ORNL DAAC), Microsoft Planetary Computer and Macrostrat, all free and without an API key.

8. Vegetation. MODIS Terra NDVI (250 m) replaces the literature value for "no vegetation".

9. Measured ground. Ground ice: mean MODIS land-surface temperature (12 months of 2023) plus ESA WorldCover permanent snow and ice. Loose soil: JAXA ALOS PALSAR L-band radar, where fine loose material looks dark, the same physics LRO Mini-RF uses on the Moon. Basalt, salts and lake sediments: Macrostrat geologic maps plus JRC Global Surface Water (1984–2021).

10. Processes, not only places. Seven processes (running water, evaporation, wind, ice, volcanism, temperature cycles and impacts), active today or long ago. The verdict shows which ones a site shares with its destination, and what watching them on Earth can teach.

11. Global map. The whole land surface scored on a 2.5° grid of NASA POWER climate. The best areas more than 700 km from any known analog are listed as new candidates.

12. Get to know the place. A credited photo, the Wikipedia summary, and a slider that compares 40 × 40 km of the Earth site (Landsat or MODIS) with the Moon or Mars site (LRO WAC or Viking, from NASA Trek) at the same scale.

13. Reverse twin. Start from any place on Earth and the app tells you which Moon or Mars site it resembles.

14. Where NASA trains. 12 sites in our catalogue that NASA or NASA-funded teams have used carry a NASA badge and a credited photo from the NASA Image and Video Library. One of them is Holuhraun in Iceland, where the Artemis II crew trained in geology in 2024. The Top 10 tab shows how our ranking places each one for your mission. It also lists 7 NASA sites outside the catalogue that can be measured live, and marks closed habitats (HI-SEAS, NEEMO, HERA/CHAPEA) as isolation analogs, not terrain analogs.

Benefits

- Mission teams get a measurable, explained reason to choose a test site, and they also see what it cannot test.

- It helps field scientists find places that have not been studied as analogs yet.

- It is open and reproducible: it runs from static files, needs no API key, and our pipeline rebuilds every dataset from public archives.

Findings

- Lunar lava-tube base (Mare Tranquillitatis pit, caves mission): Harrat Khaybar and the Umm Jirsan lava tube in Saudi Arabia score 64/100, a dry basaltic field almost never used as a space analog.

- Ice at Arcadia Planitia, Mars (ISRU): the Changtang Plateau in Tibet ranks #1, with 52 kPa air pressure, permafrost and a dry climate.

- Lunar south pole (polar light): the McMurdo Dry Valleys and the Miller Range blue-ice fields, which nobody uses yet, come out on top. Combining McMurdo, Dome C and Aorounga covers 96% of the destination.

- Jezero Crater (astrobiology): Gilf Kebir and Aorounga in the Sahara stand out, together with Licancabur.

- Compared with NASA's choices: for the lunar south pole (polar power) our #1 is the McMurdo Dry Valleys, and for Meridiani Planum (astrobiology) it is Salar de Pajonales. NASA-funded teams already work at both.

- Validation: on its own, the reverse twin pairs the Atacama Desert with Meridiani Planum, a pairing scientists already use for sulfates and perchlorates.

- Ecuador: the Galápagos volcanoes Sierra Negra (#5) and Fernandina (#6) are in the world top 10 for the lunar lava-tube pit, and Arenal del Chimborazo (4,300 m, 3 hours from Quito) is #7 for building habitats at Gale Crater.

- When we replaced five estimated characteristics with measurements, these results kept their places.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; globe.gl and three.js for the 3D globes; Web Audio and Web Speech for sound and voice; Python 3 with NumPy and Pillow for the data pipeline; the Microsoft Planetary Computer data API; Node.js for automated tests.

What makes it creative

We treat choosing an analog site as a recommendation problem, with comparable measurements on three worlds. The question changes from "which famous site?" to "which combination of sites covers this mission, and what is left out?". The result is told as a mission: launch, journey, landing and verdict.

Limitations

- Impact craters and caves still come from published studies, because they cannot be detected from orbit everywhere. Outside the USA, geologic maps are coarse, so salts and sediments keep published values there.

- Cold ground suggests permafrost but does not prove there is ice, and radar also reads salt flats as loose soil.

- Mars Odyssey sees only the top meter at low resolution, and NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide.

- Our scores support decisions. They do not certify sites.

What we hope to achieve

- A clear, repeatable way to compare analog sites that any team can check and extend.

- More field work in places nobody uses yet, including accessible ones in Latin America such as the Galápagos lava fields and the Chimborazo ash plains.

- Students and the public seeing, in English and Spanish, how open NASA data becomes a real mission decision.
